parts.text:
1
Which quantity is a physical quantity?
A
atomic number
B
efficiency
C
number density of charge carriers
D
strain

hints: Recall the syllabus test for a physical quantity: it must have a numerical magnitude that can be measured and a unit, not just a pure number.
Compare the four terms: atomic number counts protons, efficiency compares two powers or energies, strain compares two lengths, while number density of charge carriers is carriers per unit volume.
Check for a unit: a per-unit-volume quantity must have unit $\text{m}^{-3}$, whereas a count and the two ratios in this list are dimensionless.
walkthrough: State the rule used in this topic: a physical quantity has a magnitude and an associated unit in which it is measured.
Check atomic number: it is $Z$, the integer number of protons. It has a value but no unit, so it fails the test.

Check efficiency and strain: efficiency is a ratio of energies or powers and strain is $\Delta L / L$. In both cases the units on top and bottom cancel, leaving dimensionless pure numbers with no unit.
Check number density of charge carriers $n$: it is defined as number $N$ divided by volume $V$, so $n = N/V$ with unit $\text{m}^{-3}$. It has both a measurable magnitude and a unit.
Therefore only number density satisfies the definition. This is option C.

A.explanation: Atomic number is a count of protons in a nucleus. It is a pure number with no unit.

B.explanation: Efficiency is $\text{useful output} / \text{total input}$. The units cancel so it is a dimensionless ratio with no unit.

C.explanation: Number density $n = N/V$ is number per unit volume with unit $\text{m}^{-3}$. It has magnitude and unit so it is a physical quantity.

D.explanation: Strain is $\text{extension} / \text{original length}$. It is a length divided by a length so it has no unit.
